title: Tilāḥ kṛṣṇāḥ: sesame for cleansing
theme: Sesame, black and white, is offered to cleanse the speaker of wrong, to quiet a list of grave sins named one by one, and to ask Agni for the goods of a good life.

words.context: anon: «केचित्कृष्णाः केचिच्छ्वेता उभयविधाः» — some black, some white, both kinds
anon: «सौम्या रोगाद्युपद्रवाप्रदाः» — bringing no harm such as disease
anon: «वशानुगा अस्मद्वशवर्तिनः» — in our control, i.e. rightly acquired
anon: «मे मां तिलाः पुनन्तु» — may the sesame purify me

words.role: object (with mayi: the sin in me)

words.meaning: the first śrāddha (food at a recent death rite)
words.context: anon: «नवश्राद्धमेकोद्दिष्टाद्यन्नभोजनम्» — eating food at the ekoddiṣṭa and similar rites

words.role: item (a sinner named for his sin)

words.meaning: one who violates the teacher’s bed

words.context: anon: «भ्रूणो गर्भः शिशुर्वीरो वा» — bhrūṇa is an embryo, a child or a hero
anon: «त्वदाज्ञया तिला» — the sesame, by your command
anon: «एतन्मन्त्रोक्तानां पापानां शान्तिं विनाशं शमयन्तु कुर्वन्तु» — may they bring about the end of the sins named in this mantra
anon: «प्रज्ञा कुशाग्रबुद्धित्वम्» — a mind sharp as the tip of kuśa grass
anon: «तुरेवार्थे» — tu in the sense of eva
anon: «हे परमात्मंस्तत्सर्वं भवान्मह्यं सम्यग्ददातु» — may you, the Supreme, grant me all that

sandhi.rule: kṛṣṇāḥ + tilāḥ → kṛṣṇās tilāḥ: the visarga becomes s before t.
saumyāḥ + vaśānugāḥ → saumyā vaśānugāḥ: after ā the visarga drops before a voiced sound.

sandhi.type: m before c; t before d
sandhi.rule: kim + cit → kiñcit (m as the palatal nasal); cit + duritam → cid duritam.
tilāḥ + śāntim is printed tilā śāntiṃ, without the visarga; classical sandhi keeps it (tilāḥ śāntim or tilāś śāntim). See sandhi_exceptions.

sandhi_exceptions.note: tilāḥ śāntim is printed तिला शान्तिं; the anonymous commentator’s text has the same «तिला*», with a mark in the print. The analysis keeps the plural tilāḥ the verb requires.

samasa.meaning: one who goes to the teacher’s bed

morphology.note: The enclitic me can be genitive or accusative; the commentator takes it as the object, ‘me’: «मे मां तिलाः पुनन्तु».
Nominative of brahmahan, ‘slayer of a brāhmaṇa’; the list mixes the sins (theft, drinking) with the sinners named for them.
In this list śrīḥ, lakṣmīḥ and prajñā have the form of the nominative where the parallel list in 10.63 has accusatives (śriyam, lakṣmim); with sandadātu they are the things to be granted.
Accusative plural of puṣṭi, ‘kinds of nourishment’; 10.63 has the singular puṣṭim.
Vocative of jātavedas, Agni ‘who knows all born things’, with a 3rd-person imperative (sandadātu): the commentator renders it with the polite bhavān, ‘may you grant’.

translation.literal: Sesame seeds [are] black, sesame seeds [are] white, sesame seeds [are] gentle, obedient. May the sesame seeds purify me — the sin, whatever wrong [is] in me. Svāhā. A thief’s food, the first śrāddha, the slayer of a brāhmaṇa, the violator of the teacher’s bed, theft of cattle, drinking liquor, killing an embryo — may the sesame seeds bring [these] to rest. Svāhā. Prosperity and fortune and nourishments and good name and freedom from debt, piety, many children, faith and intelligence, wisdom — O Jātavedas, may [you] grant [these]. Svāhā.
translation.readable: Black sesame, white sesame, gentle and rightly ours: may this sesame cleanse me of whatever wrong is in me. Svāhā. Food taken from a thief, food eaten at a first death-rite, the killing of a brāhmaṇa, the violation of the teacher’s bed, cattle-theft, drinking liquor, the killing of an embryo — may the sesame bring all this to rest. Svāhā. Prosperity and fortune, nourishment and a good name, freedom from debt, piety, many children, faith, understanding and wisdom — Agni, knower of all, grant them. Svāhā.

syntax: Three offering formulas closed by svāhā. The first is a series of nominal sentences (tilāḥ kṛṣṇāḥ …) followed by an imperative (punantu) with the enclitic me and a relative clause (yat kiṃcid duritaṃ mayi). The second is a list of seven sins in the nominative followed by tilāḥ śāntiṃ śamayantu, ‘may the sesame bring [them] to rest’. The third repeats the list of goods from 10.63, now addressed to Agni with the vocative jātavedaḥ and the imperative sandadātu.

ambiguities.note: The text lists the sins and the sinners together (corasyānnam, navaśrāddham, brahmahā, gurutalpagaḥ, gosteyam, surāpānam, bhrūṇahatyā). The commentator reads them as the sins whose ‘end’ the sesame should bring about.
An embryo, a child, or (in older usage) a learned brāhmaṇa; the commentator gives three senses: «भ्रूणो गर्भः शिशुर्वीरो वा».
The commentator answers that inert seeds can remove sin only by the Supreme’s command: «अचेतनानां तिलानां पापनाशनसामर्थ्यं त्वदाज्ञयेति भावः». The text does not say.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Anuṣṭubh-like half-verses with svāhā and prose: the five printed lines count 16, 34, 35, 8 and 17 syllables (the second and third each contain two half-verses and a svāhā).

beginner: This formula goes with an offering of sesame seeds, black and white, into the fire. The speaker asks the sesame to cleanse whatever wrong is in him. Then come seven grave wrongs named one after another — eating food from a thief, eating at a first death-rite, killing a brāhmaṇa, violating the teacher’s bed, stealing cattle, drinking liquor, killing an unborn child — and a request that the sesame bring them to rest. Last, Agni the fire god is asked for prosperity, a good name, freedom from debt, children, faith and wisdom. The old commentator explains that seeds by themselves have no power over sin; they act by the command of the Supreme. The edition reports these readings and makes no claim about what the rite achieves.
analogy: Like handing over a written list of debts to be settled, item by item, before asking for anything new.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Sesame, black and white, gentle and ‘obedient’, is asked to purify the speaker of whatever wrong is in him; seven grave sins are named and the sesame is asked to bring them to rest; and Agni Jātavedas is asked to grant prosperity, fortune, nourishment, good name, freedom from debt, piety, many children, faith, intelligence and wisdom. Each formula ends with svāhā.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read the sesame?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The seeds are of both colours and harmless, «केचित्कृष्णाः केचिच्छ्वेता उभयविधाः सर्वेऽपि सौम्या रोगाद्युपद्रवाप्रदाः»; ‘obedient’ means rightly acquired, not stolen: «स्वधर्मोपार्जितं द्रव्यं दत्त्वा विक्रीयाऽऽनीता». They purify only by the Supreme’s command: «अचेतनानां तिलानां पापनाशनसामर्थ्यं त्वदाज्ञयेति भावः».

commentary.q: How does he gloss the sins?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He explains only what needs it: the first śrāddha is eating at the ekoddiṣṭa and similar rites, «नवश्राद्धमेकोद्दिष्टाद्यन्नभोजनम्», and bhrūṇa has three senses, «भ्रूणो गर्भः शिशुर्वीरो वा»; the rest he calls clear. The request is that the sesame bring about the end of these sins: «एतन्मन्त्रोक्तानां पापानां शान्तिं विनाशं शमयन्तु कुर्वन्तु».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The Chāndogya names four men who fall — the thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the teacher’s bed and the slayer of a brāhmaṇa — and a fifth who keeps company with them. Three of those four stand in this list; the Chāndogya’s thief of gold corresponds here to cattle-theft and a thief’s food.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: the anonymous bhāṣya reads it as a ritual formula, and neither Sāyaṇa nor Bhāskara comments on it in the copies used (their 64-anuvāka texts do not include it). Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary is not in the sources. No school position is given.

parallels.note: The Chāndogya’s list of those who fall shares three of this anuvāka’s sins: violating the teacher’s bed, killing a brāhmaṇa, and drinking liquor.

contemporary.text: The anuvāka does not leave wrongdoing vague: it names seven specific acts before asking for anything. Naming wrongs one by one, rather than in general, is a recognisable step in taking responsibility. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a rite name each wrong separately instead of saying ‘all my wrongs’?
reflect.deeper: The commentator insists that the seeds act only by the Supreme’s command. What would be lost if the ritual object were thought to work by itself?
reflect.practice: Write down one specific thing you would like to put right, in one plain sentence.

references.text: Only the anonymous bhāṣya comments on this anuvāka in the edition’s sources; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s 64-anuvāka texts do not include it in the copies used.

flags.note: tilā śāntiṃ is printed without the visarga the plural requires; it is declared as an exception, not corrected. The Tirupati e-text adds a svāhā at the end of 10.63 before this anuvāka.
The list’s mixture of sins and sinners, and the senses of bhrūṇa, are read by the commentator as reported; the edition does not adopt his social glosses.
